notes:
I've put together notes on Psalm 99. There are some gaps. I didn't find any Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal, Orthodox or modern popular-teaching (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace) material on this psalm, so none appears below. The only real disagreement between traditions that I found is over the "footstool" in v. 5 (Augustine against Calvin, with Gill in between). Augustine's sermon is listed under the Latin numbering (Psalm 98), and the page cut off partway through, at v. 4.

**Whole psalm**
- Guzik calls it a threefold announcement that God is holy, like Isaiah 6:3. Each section ends with the refrain "He is holy," which he compares to Isaiah 6:3 and Revelation 4:8.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/
- Matthew Henry says that while the psalms just before this one look ahead to the gospel age, this one seems to dwell more upon the Old-Testament dispensation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_099.cfm
- Spurgeon's collection notes that this is the third and last psalm to open with "The LORD reigneth" (93, 97, 99).  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps099.cfm
- The Expositor's Bible says the psalm goes beyond the other "LORD reigns" psalms to the principle behind God's rule, namely, holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/99.htm

**v. 1**
- Guzik: God is not simply present; He is a reigning king. He says the throne could be the heavenly sanctuary or the earthly tabernacle or temple, and both are true and either one fits. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/
- Spurgeon: God's people should feel a solemn yet joyful awe. He links the cherubim with the mercy-seat, God's throne of grace which is sprinkled with atoning blood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-1.htm
- Ellicott: the Greek (LXX) and Latin (Vulgate) translations read "be angry" instead of "tremble." The Hebrew is a plain present, the peoples tremble, the earth staggers. https://biblehub.com/psalms/99-1.htm
- Calvin says the verbs can be read as future, so the passage may be regarded as a prediction of the subjection of the heathen world to the dominion of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/99.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): he follows the "be angry" reading and applies it to idol-worshippers angered when Christ was preached. He calls it a prediction, not a command. He also says a loving soul becomes God's throne. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801099.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: God is present everywhere but has special regard for Zion. Quoting Poole, he notes the Hebrew word order is "The Lord in Zion… is great."  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/
- Spurgeon applies Zion to the church, his church is now his favoured palace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-1.htm
- Augustine says Zion means "watching." He concludes that Zion, the city of God, is the Holy Church. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801099.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: holiness at root means being set apart. It is the essence of His entire Being, not one trait among others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/
- Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary prefer "Holy is He" to "it [the name] is holy," because the same refrain in vv. 5 and 9 needs "He." Ellicott joins vv. 3 and 4 into one cry of praise.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-3.htm
- The Expositor's Bible says it makes no difference to the meaning which way the refrain is read.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/99.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: God's power could in theory be used for evil, Yet Yahweh the King loves justice and has established equity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/
- Barnes: no one could praise a being of mere power. Praise fits only when that power always serves what is right.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-4.htm
- On who "the King" is, readings differ. Cambridge and the Pulpit Commentary say it is the LORD himself. Matthew Henry thinks it may be David, as a type of Christ. Gill applies it to Christ.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-4.htm and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_099.cfm
- Augustine: God himself works judgment (telling good from evil) and righteousness (doing good) in us. We cannot produce them on our own.  https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801099.htm

**v. 5 (the main point of disagreement)**
- Traditional view: most commentators take the footstool to be the ark of the covenant (Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary says that everywhere except Isaiah 66:1 the footstool is the ark.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/ and  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-5.htm
- Cambridge (modern-critical): since there was no ark in the Second Temple, the temple itself, or perhaps Zion, must be meant.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-5.htm
- Catholic (Augustine): he asks how one can worship the earth, God's footstool, without idolatry. His answer is that Christ took upon Him earth from earth, meaning his flesh from Mary. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801099.htm
- Reformed (Calvin): he calls Augustine's answer ingenious but reads the verse differently. Calling the temple God's footstool was meant to elevate their thoughts above it, guarding against superstition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/99-5.html
- Baptist (Gill), in between: he allows that the ark may be meant as a type of Christ's human nature. He stresses that the text says worship *at* the footstool, not worship *of* it.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/99-5.html
- Trapp (Puritan) reports Augustine's view. He says Christ's humanity is not adored in itself, but only as united in one person with his divinity.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-99.cfm
- Coffman takes the footstool to be the whole earth, so God may be worshipped anywhere.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/99-5.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik: Moses, Aaron and Samuel are named as men who prayed and were answered. Quoting VanGemeren, he says "priests" is used loosely here for servants or intercessors.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/
- Spurgeon: Though not ordained to the typical priesthood, Moses was a true priest, even as Melchizedek had been before him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps099.cfm
- Ellicott thinks the poet is honouring the priests of his own day by comparing them to past heroes, as one might say "we have a Newton among us."  https://biblehub.com/psalms/99-6.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch reject the view of the older scholar Hitzig that the three are interceding from heaven. They take vv. 6–7 as looking back to the past, applying to the whole nation of "priests and praying ones."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-7.htm

**v. 7**
- Benson and Poole: Scripture never says God spoke to Samuel from the cloud. They suggest the thunder at Mizpeh (1 Samuel 7) implies a cloud.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-7.htm
- Barnes says this can't be literally true of Samuel, unless the "pillar" is taken broadly to mean the cloud of God's presence.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-7.htm
- Cambridge: the second line states the condition of prevailing prayer, which is obeying what God has revealed. Spurgeon links this to John 15:7.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-7.htm and  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps099.cfm
- Gill: the cloudy pillar was a type of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Commentators disagree over who "them" is:
  - Guzik says most commentators mean Israel, though Moses, Aaron and Samuel were each disciplined too.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-99/
  - Benson prefers the people, since the three prayed for the people's pardon, not their own.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-8.htm
  - Spurgeon calls the Samuel version of the "three were punished" view a very doubtful statement. Another writer he quotes accepts it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps099.cfm
- Maclaren (in the Expositor's Bible): a holy God forgives, but pardon is bound up with retribution, because God loves too well to grant impunity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/99.htm
- Maclaren also says the word "though" is commentary rather than translation, and that divine "vengeance" must not be read as personal retaliation.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-8.htm
- Cambridge: pardoning God must still chastise, lest men should imagine that He makes light of sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-8.htm

**v. 9**
- Barnes: the "holy hill" is Zion, the centre of national worship. Ending on God's holiness gives the reason for worship.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-9.htm
- Gill applies the hill to the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/99-9.htm
- Maclaren: adding "our God" to "holy" bridges the gap, so that bowing low and approaching with confidence go together.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/99.htm
